name: Arm Triangle from High Mount
description: Master the arm triangle choke from high mount in BJJ. Step-by-step guide covering setup, grip transitions, finishing angles, defensive counters, and safety.
target_area: Carotid arteries (compressed by opponent's own shoulder and your arm)
summary: The arm triangle from high mount is a head-and-arm blood choke that traps the defender's own arm across their neck and compresses both carotids—their trapped shoulder on one side, your forearm on the other—to finish from grappling's most dominant mount.
overview:
The arm triangle from high mount exploits the most dominant mount variation to isolate the defender's arm against their own neck, creating a bilateral carotid compression using the opponent's trapped shoulder and the attacker's forearm. High mount provides decisive advantages for this submission: the elevated knee position near the armpits restricts the defender's arm movement, gravity assists in steering the arm across the face, and the compressed posture limits defensive bridging and framing.

The setup typically begins when the attacker uses cross-face pressure or capitalizes on the defender's arm frames to push the near arm across the centerline of the neck. Once the arm is positioned, the attacker threads their choking arm over the trapped arm and behind the defender's head, locks a figure-four or gable grip, and transitions to a perpendicular finishing angle by stepping over to side control. The high mount entry is particularly effective because defenders are already compromised with limited escape options and restricted mobility.

Strategically, the arm triangle from high mount integrates seamlessly into systematic mount attack chains. Armbar threats force defenders to retract their arms, positioning them for the arm triangle push across the neck. Choke threats force defenders to extend and frame, creating armbar opportunities that cycle back to arm triangle setups when the arms retract again. This cyclical pressure dynamic makes the arm triangle from high mount a high-percentage finish in competition and training alike, serving as a cornerstone of methodical mount finishing sequences used by elite grapplers.

injury_risks.injury: Loss of consciousness from blood choke
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery if released promptly; potential stroke risk if held too long

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain from improper pressure angle
Shoulder compression injury to trapped arm

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum from lock to tap. Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness in 6-8 seconds.
tap_signals: Physical hand tap (multiple taps on opponent or mat)
Physical foot tap (multiple taps with foot)
Any distress signal or loss of resistance
Immediately release if opponent goes limp
release_protocol: Immediately release arm squeeze and remove head pressure
Step back from opponent's head and shoulders
Allow opponent to breathe and recover (30-60 seconds)
Check for consciousness and normal breathing
If unconscious: position on side, elevate legs, monitor breathing until conscious
training_restrictions: Never spike or jerk the submission - apply smooth progressive pressure only
Never hold after tap signal - release immediately upon any tap
Always allow tap access - do not trap both arms in training
Never use competition speed in training - practice control first
Stop immediately if opponent's face changes color (purple/red indicates excessive pressure)

variations_and_setups.description: The most direct entry where the attacker uses cross-face pressure from high mount to drive the opponent's near arm across their own neck. The attacker's forearm slides across the defender's jaw and pushes the arm into position, then the choking arm threads behind the neck to establish the head-and-arm lock.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent keeps their arms close to their body defending chokes and you can establish strong cross-face control

variations_and_setups.description: The attacker baits the opponent into creating a defensive frame against the chest or neck from high mount. When the defender pushes their forearm across to create distance, the attacker pins the framing arm with chest pressure and immediately transitions to the head-and-arm configuration by threading over the trapped arm.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent actively frames against your chest or neck from high mount bottom, turning their defensive action into the arm triangle setup

variations_and_setups.description: After establishing the head-and-arm lock from high mount, the attacker steps over and walks their hips to a perpendicular side control angle before applying the final squeeze. This provides maximum chest compression and eliminates the space the opponent needs to defend or breathe.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against larger or more flexible opponents who can create space when you attempt to finish from the mounted angle

attacker.name: from High Mount Attacker
attacker.description: Step-by-step guide to finishing the arm triangle from high mount. Learn setup mechanics, grip transitions, finishing angles, and systematic attack chains from mount.
attacker.overview: The arm triangle from high mount leverages your dominant elevated position to isolate the defender's arm against their own neck, then finish with chest-to-chest compression. From high mount, you already control the opponent's upper body with your knees near their armpits, severely limiting their defensive options. The setup involves pushing or steering the defender's near arm across their face using cross-face pressure, weight distribution, or by capitalizing on their defensive frames. Once the arm is trapped, you thread your choking arm behind their neck, establish a figure-four grip, and transition to a perpendicular finishing angle—typically moving to side control. The key advantage of entering from high mount is that the opponent's limited mobility and your gravitational advantage make arm isolation significantly easier than from other positions, and the natural forward weight distribution maintains constant pressure throughout the entire transition sequence.
key_principles: Use cross-face pressure and forward weight to steer the opponent's arm across their own neck rather than muscling it into position
Pin the trapped arm with chest weight before transitioning to the head-and-arm grip to prevent extraction during the vulnerable grip switch
Walk hips to a perpendicular angle on the trapped-arm side before applying the finishing squeeze for optimal carotid compression
Generate choking pressure through chest compression and hip drop rather than arm squeezing to maintain sustainable finishing force
Keep your head low and sealed to the mat on the far side to eliminate space and prevent the opponent from turning away from the choke
Chain the arm triangle with other high mount attacks—armbar threats force arm retraction into arm triangle range creating cyclical pressure
setup_requirements: Established high mount position with knees near opponent's armpits and forward weight distribution on upper chest
Opponent's near arm positioned across their own neck through cross-face pressure or caught during a defensive frame attempt
Sufficient upper body control preventing the opponent from bridging or sitting up during the grip transition phase
Your weight distributed forward on the opponent's upper chest to maintain crushing pressure during the transition to head-and-arm control

execution_steps.action: Isolate the near arm across the neck
execution_steps.description: From high mount, use cross-face pressure or frame-trapping to push the opponent's near arm across their own neck. Your forearm drives across their jaw line while your weight pins them flat. The arm must cross their centerline so their own shoulder will compress one carotid artery. Do not rush this step—methodical pressure is more effective than explosive force.

execution_steps.action: Pin the trapped arm with chest pressure
execution_steps.description: Before adjusting your grip, drive your chest forward and down onto the opponent's trapped arm, pinning it firmly against their neck with your body weight. Your sternum should press directly onto their forearm or bicep, immobilizing the arm through compression rather than grip strength alone. This prevents the opponent from retracting the arm during the grip transition.

execution_steps.action: Thread the choking arm behind the neck
execution_steps.description: Slide your choking-side arm over the top of the opponent's trapped arm and behind the back of their neck. Your forearm blade should cross behind the neck pressing against the far-side carotid artery. Move smoothly and maintain chest pressure throughout—any gap created during threading allows the opponent to extract their arm and reset the defense.

execution_steps.action: Lock the figure-four or gable grip
execution_steps.description: Connect your hands by gripping your own bicep with the choking hand while your free hand cups behind the opponent's head, creating a tight figure-four lock. Alternatively, use a gable grip for maximum compression. The grip must lock the opponent's head and trapped arm together as a single unit with zero slack in the configuration.

execution_steps.action: Step over and walk to the finishing angle
execution_steps.description: Step your leg over the opponent's body and walk your hips around toward the trapped-arm side until you are perpendicular to their body. Your chest should be directly over their face. Each step tightens the choke by removing available space between your bodies. The perpendicular angle ensures the opponent's shoulder drives maximally into their own carotid.

execution_steps.action: Drop hip and seal the position
execution_steps.description: Drop your hip closest to the trapped arm to the mat, sprawling your weight onto the opponent. Your head drops low to the mat on the far side of their head, sealing the position completely. This removes the space opponents use to breathe or create defensive frames. Your body acts as a wall preventing any rotation or escape movement.

Expand your chest while pulling your elbows together toward your own centerline. The opponent's trapped shoulder compresses one carotid artery while your forearm blade compresses the other. Apply slow, steady, progressive pressure rather than explosive squeezing. The choke tightens with each exhale the opponent makes. Wait patiently for the tap or feel resistance fade as blood restriction takes effect.

common_counters.counter: Opponent retracts trapped arm before the head-and-arm grip is locked
common_counters.your_response: If the arm clears during the grip transition, immediately re-establish high mount control and return to cross-face pressure. Reset the arm isolation using methodical pressure rather than chasing the arm. The high mount position remains dominant even when the submission fails.

common_counters.counter: Opponent bridges explosively toward the choking arm side during the transition
common_counters.your_response: Post your far-side hand wide and drop your hip to absorb the bridge. If the bridge is powerful enough to displace you, maintain the head-and-arm grip through the roll and finish from bottom using a guard arm triangle configuration. Do not release the grip during the bridge.

common_counters.counter: Opponent creates a far-arm frame to prevent chest-to-chest compression at the finishing angle
common_counters.your_response: Use your free hand to swim inside their far-side elbow and strip the frame. Walk your hips further toward their head to collapse the space their frame creates. The perpendicular angle makes their frame progressively weaker as you advance past it.

common_counters.counter: Opponent hip escapes and recovers closed guard during the step-over transition
common_counters.your_response: Maintain the head-and-arm grip and work to pass their guard or open their legs by posting your knee into their tailbone. The arm triangle grip remains effective even inside guard if you can establish the finishing angle. Avoid releasing the grip to pass—instead, pass while maintaining the lock.

common_errors.error: Releasing cross-face pressure too early before chest weight secures the trapped arm against the neck
common_errors.consequence: Opponent retracts their arm freely during the transition, escaping the arm triangle setup entirely and returning to standard high mount defense
common_errors.correction: Pin the opponent's arm with your chest weight before releasing cross-face pressure. The arm must be immobilized by body compression before you initiate the grip switch to the head-and-arm configuration.

common_errors.error: Squeezing with arms instead of using chest compression and body angle to generate pressure
common_errors.consequence: Arms fatigue rapidly, the choke becomes ineffective, and the opponent can endure the pressure long enough to work an escape or wait for you to gas out
common_errors.correction: Walk to a perpendicular angle and use your dropping hip and expanding chest to generate pressure. Your arms lock the configuration in place while your body creates the compressive force through structure and gravity.

common_errors.error: Leaving space between your chest and the opponent's trapped shoulder during the finish
common_errors.consequence: The opponent can breathe through the choke and create incremental space to extract their arm or work defensive frames against the compression
common_errors.correction: Drop your weight directly onto the opponent's trapped shoulder and face. Your chest must be flush against their body with zero gap. Think about melting your weight through them rather than hovering above the position.

common_errors.error: Failing to walk hips to a perpendicular angle before attempting the squeeze
common_errors.consequence: The choke is applied at a suboptimal angle where the opponent's shoulder does not properly compress the carotid, resulting in a neck crank rather than a clean blood choke
common_errors.correction: Complete the full hip walk-around until you are at a 90-degree angle to the opponent's body. The chest-to-face alignment at perpendicular is what makes the opponent's own shoulder do the choking work through bilateral carotid compression.

common_errors.error: Keeping head high instead of dropping it to the mat on the far side of the opponent's head
common_errors.consequence: Creates a gap on the far side that the opponent can use to turn their head and relieve pressure or work their arm free through the created space
common_errors.correction: Drop your head to the mat on the far side of the opponent's head immediately after walking to the finishing angle. Your head acts as a seal that prevents the opponent from turning away from the choke.

common_errors.error: Attempting the arm triangle without first establishing solid high mount control and weight distribution
common_errors.consequence: Rushing the submission from an unstable mount position gives the opponent bridging and framing opportunities that would not exist from a consolidated high mount
common_errors.correction: Consolidate high mount fully before initiating the arm triangle setup. Walk knees to armpits, establish forward weight, and confirm the opponent is flat and controlled before beginning the arm isolation sequence.

Practice the grip switch, stepping over, and walking to the perpendicular finishing angle against 30% resistance. Partner provides feedback on pressure location, grip tightness, and when the choke becomes effective. Alternate sides.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 3: Full sequence with attack chains

Practice the full arm triangle sequence including recognizing when the arm is available versus when to threaten armbars or chokes to create the arm triangle opening. If the arm triangle fails, flow to armbar or return to mount pressure. 3-minute rounds.

Practice the complete sequence: isolate arm, transition grip, walk to angle, finish. Chain with armbars and chokes when the arm triangle is defended. 5-minute rounds with full reset on escape or submission.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the arm triangle from high mount attack?
flashcards.answer: The arm triangle compresses both carotid arteries simultaneously using a bilateral compression mechanism. The opponent's own trapped shoulder presses into one carotid from the near side, driven by chest-to-chest compression, while the attacker's forearm blade crosses behind the neck and presses into the opposite carotid from the far side. This bilateral restriction of blood flow to the brain causes unconsciousness in 6-8 seconds if not released.

flashcards.question: Your opponent tucks their elbows tight to defend armbar attempts from high mount - how do you create the arm triangle setup?
flashcards.answer: When the opponent tucks their elbows defensively, use cross-face pressure to push their near arm across their own neck. Slide your forearm across their jaw line while driving your weight forward, steering the arm past their centerline. The tucked elbow position actually assists this push because the arm is already close to the neck. Once the arm crosses their centerline, immediately pin it with chest pressure before they can retract it.

plausible: Wait for them to extend arm
trap: Yank the wrist to free it

flashcards.question: What grip configuration locks the head-and-arm position for the arm triangle finish?
flashcards.answer: The primary grip is a figure-four lock: the choking hand grips your own opposite bicep while your free hand cups behind the opponent's head, creating a closed loop around their head and trapped arm. Alternatively, a gable grip (palm-to-palm) provides maximum initial compression but offers less structural security. The figure-four is preferred because it locks mechanically and prevents the opponent from creating space by pushing on your hands.

flashcards.question: You have locked the head-and-arm grip from high mount but the opponent bridges explosively to prevent you from stepping over - what adjustment do you make?
flashcards.answer: Post your far-side hand wide on the mat and drop your base low to absorb the bridge rather than fighting it rigidly. If the bridge is strong enough to roll you, maintain the head-and-arm grip through the transition and finish from bottom position using a guard arm triangle. Do not release the grip to rebase. If the bridge fails, immediately step over and walk to the perpendicular finishing angle before the opponent can generate another explosive bridge attempt.

plausible: Fight the bridge with pure strength
trap: Release grip to stop the roll

flashcards.question: What body angle creates maximum finishing pressure for the arm triangle from high mount?
flashcards.answer: Walk your hips until they are perpendicular—90 degrees—to the opponent's body on the trapped-arm side. Drop your near hip to the mat and place your head on the mat on the far side of their head. Your chest should be directly over their face. This angle allows your expanding chest and body weight to drive the opponent's shoulder bone into their own carotid while your forearm compresses the other side. Any angle less than perpendicular reduces shoulder-on-carotid compression and may produce a neck crank rather than a clean blood choke.

flashcards.question: During the grip transition from high mount to arm triangle, the opponent starts pulling their trapped arm free - what is your immediate response?
flashcards.answer: If the arm is sliding free during the grip transition, do not chase the arm triangle from a compromised position. Instead, immediately drive your chest weight back down onto the arm to re-pin it, or release the transition entirely and return to consolidated high mount control. From high mount you can re-isolate the arm using cross-face pressure once the position is stabilized. Forcing a grip transition on a partially freed arm results in a loose, ineffective choke that wastes energy and position.

flashcards.question: What are the key indicators that the arm triangle is properly locked and the opponent is approaching the point of no escape?
flashcards.answer: The choke is properly locked when you feel the opponent's trapped shoulder bone pressing firmly into their neck with no space between your chest and their body. Their face may begin changing color as blood flow restricts. Their defensive movements become weaker and less coordinated, and their free arm framing loses force. If they cannot create any meaningful frame with their free hand and cannot bridge effectively to disrupt your angle, they have passed the point of no escape and the finish is imminent.
flashcards.answer_line: No space, weak frame, color change

flashcards.question: What safety precautions must you observe when applying the arm triangle from high mount in training?
flashcards.answer: Apply pressure progressively over 3-5 seconds minimum from lock to tap—never spike or jerk the submission. Monitor the opponent's consciousness by watching for facial color changes, feeling for resistance changes, and noting if their movements suddenly weaken. Always ensure at least one of the opponent's hands is free to tap. Release immediately upon any tap signal including verbal, hand, or foot taps. If the opponent goes limp, release immediately and place them in recovery position on their side with legs elevated.

plausible: Apply quickly for a fast tap
Finish even if partner can't tap
trap: Hold a few extra seconds after tap

flashcards.question: Your opponent creates a strong frame with their free arm against your shoulder to prevent chest compression at the finishing angle - how do you eliminate this defense?
flashcards.answer: Swim your free hand inside their far-side elbow to strip the frame from underneath rather than trying to muscle through it from above. Simultaneously walk your hips further toward their head, which collapses the space their frame creates and reduces their mechanical advantage. As you advance past the frame, your chest weight makes the frame progressively weaker. If the frame is extremely strong, use your head pressure on the far side to eliminate the space the frame is trying to create.

flashcards.question: How does the arm triangle from high mount integrate into systematic mount attack chains for competition finishing?
flashcards.answer: The arm triangle operates as part of a cyclical attack chain from high mount. Armbar threats force the opponent to retract and tuck their arms defensively, which positions the arms near the neck for the arm triangle push. Choke threats force the opponent to extend arms and create frames, exposing armbars. Each defense to one attack creates the setup for the next. In competition, patient practitioners use this cycle to progressively exhaust defensive options until the arm triangle or another submission in the chain succeeds.

defender.name: from High Mount Defender
defender.description: Defend the arm triangle from high mount. Recognize the setup, prevent arm isolation across your neck, and escape to safer positions before the choke locks.
defender.overview: Defending the arm triangle from high mount requires recognizing the setup before your arm is trapped against your own neck. The primary danger occurs when the attacker uses cross-face pressure or capitalizes on your defensive frames to push your near arm across your centerline. Once your arm is positioned against your own carotid and the attacker threads their choking arm behind your neck, escape difficulty increases dramatically with each subsequent step of the finishing sequence. Successful defense demands constant awareness of your arm positioning, keeping your near arm either tight against your body or fully extended away from your neck, and never allowing your forearm to cross your own throat line. Early defense during the setup phase is far more effective than attempting to escape a fully locked and sealed arm triangle, so understanding the attacker's sequence and defending at the earliest possible moment is essential for survival from this extremely dangerous position.
key_principles: Defend the arm position first - keep your near arm either fully retracted tight against your body or fully extended away, never crossing your own neck
Recognize cross-face pressure as the primary arm triangle setup and resist the push before your arm crosses centerline
Exploit the grip transition window when the attacker switches from mount control to head-and-arm grip as the highest-percentage escape moment
Turn into the attacker rather than away to prevent the perpendicular finishing angle and reduce shoulder-on-carotid compression
Frame against the attacker's hips and shoulders to prevent them from stepping over and walking to the finishing angle
Tap early and clearly when the choke is locked - arm triangles restrict blood flow rapidly with minimal warning before unconsciousness
recognition_cues: The attacker applies strong cross-face pressure driving your near arm across your face and toward your opposite shoulder from high mount
The attacker pins your arm against your neck with deliberate chest pressure and begins threading their arm over yours and behind your neck
The attacker begins stepping over your body and walking their hips toward your side while maintaining a grip around your head and arm
The attacker drops their hip to the mat and their head drops low on the far side of your head as they settle into the finishing position

defensive_options.action: Retract the near arm before the cross-face push completes the isolation
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you feel cross-face pressure beginning to push your arm across your neck before the attacker establishes chest pressure on the trapped arm
defensive_options.if_successful: Arm stays clear of the neck, attacker must reset the arm triangle setup from high mount control
defensive_options.risk: Retracting the arm may expose it to armbar attacks if the attacker reads the defensive movement

defensive_options.action: Turn into the attacker toward the trapped-arm side to prevent the perpendicular finishing angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has locked the head-and-arm grip but has not yet walked to the perpendicular angle or dropped their hip to seal
defensive_options.if_successful: Disrupts the finishing angle and can lead to the attacker returning to high mount top without the arm triangle
defensive_options.risk: Turning incorrectly toward the wrong side can accelerate the choke by driving your shoulder deeper into your own carotid

defensive_options.action: Bridge toward the trapped-arm side and recover guard during the step-over transition
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker steps over your body to walk to the finishing angle and their base is momentarily compromised during the transition
defensive_options.if_successful: Creates enough space to pull the attacker into closed guard where the arm triangle angle is disrupted and finishing becomes difficult
defensive_options.risk: A strong bridge against a well-positioned attacker may fail and waste energy needed for later defense

defensive_options.action: Hip escape and re-guard before the choke is sealed at the perpendicular angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has stepped over but is still adjusting hip position and has not dropped hip to seal
defensive_options.if_successful: Disrupts the finishing mechanics by recovering guard where the attacker cannot generate the chest compression needed for the choke
defensive_options.risk: If the choke is already tight, movement may accelerate the submission by tightening the arm triangle configuration

escape_paths: Retract the near arm before the head-and-arm grip is established and return to standard high mount bottom defense
Turn into the attacker toward the trapped-arm side and fight to knees to prevent the perpendicular finishing angle
Bridge explosively toward the trapped-arm side during the step-over transition to recover guard
Lock hands together and straighten the trapped arm to prevent the shoulder from compressing the carotid

favorable_outcomes.how: Bridge powerfully toward the trapped-arm side during the attacker's step-over transition, exploiting their momentary base compromise to sweep them into your closed guard where the arm triangle angle is neutralized.

Retract your arm during the early setup phase or the grip transition window, preventing the arm triangle from being established. The attacker returns to high mount top position and must restart their attack sequence.

common_errors.error: Allowing your near arm to cross your own neck while framing against the attacker's chest from high mount bottom
common_errors.consequence: Your defensive frame becomes the trapped arm the attacker needs for the arm triangle, directly creating the submission setup
common_errors.correction: When defending from high mount bottom, keep your near arm either pinned tight to your own body with elbow down or extended away from your neck. Use head positioning and hip movement for defense rather than arm frames across your throat line.

common_errors.error: Turning away from the attacker when caught in the arm triangle
common_errors.consequence: Turning away gives the attacker the perpendicular angle they need and drives your own shoulder deeper into your carotid, accelerating the choke significantly
common_errors.correction: Always turn into the attacker toward the trapped-arm side. This flattens the choke angle and prevents your shoulder from compressing your own carotid artery.

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to defend and trying to escape after the arm triangle is fully locked with hip dropped and head sealed
common_errors.consequence: A fully sealed arm triangle is extremely difficult to escape. You waste energy fighting a near-certain submission and risk going unconscious from the bilateral carotid compression.
common_errors.correction: Defend during the earliest possible window—resist the cross-face push, retract the arm during grip transition, or turn in before the angle is established. If the arm triangle is fully locked and sealed, tap early rather than risking unconsciousness.

common_errors.error: Pushing against the attacker's head instead of their hips when trying to create escape space
common_errors.consequence: Pushing the head does not disrupt the arm triangle mechanics and wastes arm energy that could be used for more effective escape movements like bridging or hip escaping
common_errors.correction: Frame against the attacker's hips and near-side shoulder to prevent them from walking to the perpendicular angle. Hip frames disrupt the body mechanics that generate the finishing compression, while head pushes do not affect the choke at all.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the attacker is setting up an arm triangle from high mount?
flashcards.answer: The primary recognition cue is feeling strong cross-face pressure from the attacker driving your near arm across your face toward your opposite shoulder. This differs from normal mount control because the pressure is specifically directed at pushing your arm across your neck rather than controlling your head. The second cue is feeling the attacker's chest weight deliberately pin your arm against your own neck before they begin threading their choking arm behind your head.

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap when caught in a locked arm triangle from high mount?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately and clearly using any available signal: tap the mat or the attacker's body multiple times with your free hand, tap with your feet if hands are trapped, or verbally say 'tap' loudly and clearly. Do not wait to see if you can escape once the choke is fully locked and sealed—arm triangles compress the carotid arteries and can cause unconsciousness in 6-8 seconds with minimal warning signs. Tapping early prevents injury and allows you to continue training safely.
flashcards.answer_line: Tap early, any signal, don't wait

plausible: Wait to see if you can escape

flashcards.question: What arm positioning prevents the attacker from setting up the arm triangle from high mount?
flashcards.answer: Keep your near arm either pinned tight against your own body with your elbow down and hand on your own chest, or extend it fully away from your neck in a direction that does not cross your throat line. The critical mistake is allowing your forearm to cross your own centerline at neck level, which creates the trapped-arm position the attacker needs. When defending high mount, prioritize hip escapes and bridges for escape rather than arm frames that cross your neck.
flashcards.answer_line: Keep arm off your own neck

flashcards.question: The attacker has locked the head-and-arm grip but has not yet stepped over to the finishing angle - what escape options remain?
flashcards.answer: This is your last high-percentage escape window. Turn into the attacker toward your trapped-arm side and fight to get to your knees, which prevents them from establishing the perpendicular finishing angle. Simultaneously frame against their hips with your free arm to prevent them from stepping over. If you can face into the attacker, they cannot generate the chest compression needed to finish. Alternatively, bridge explosively toward the trapped-arm side during their step-over attempt to recover guard.
flashcards.answer_line: Turn in, get to knees, frame hips

flashcards.question: Why is turning toward the attacker more effective than turning away when defending the arm triangle?
flashcards.answer: Turning toward the attacker (into the trapped-arm side) flattens the angle between your bodies, which reduces the compression of your own shoulder against your carotid artery. It also prevents the attacker from achieving the perpendicular finishing angle they need for maximum chest compression. Turning away from the attacker does the opposite—it drives your trapped shoulder deeper into your own carotid, gives the attacker the perpendicular angle, and accelerates the choke rather than relieving it.
